props.title: Running on Karma

sections.content: **Running on Karma** (2003) represents a fascinating pivot point in Hong Kong cinema, blending supernatural elements with action in ways that broke new ground. Andy Lau's portrayal of a Buddhist monk-turned-stripper who can see people's karma marks a departure from traditional Hong Kong action films like **Police Story** (1985) or **Once Upon a Time in China** (1991). Directors Johnnie To and Wai Ka-Fai crafted a unique spiritual thriller that arrived during Hong Kong cinema's post-handover soul-searching period, alongside works like **Internal Affairs** (2002) and **2046** (2004).

sections.content: The film's ambitious mixing of genres exemplifies Hong Kong cinema's early 2000s experimentation. While earlier films like **Mr. Vampire** (1985) combined horror and kung fu, **Running on Karma** pushes further by integrating Buddhist philosophy, romance, and police procedural elements. The prosthetic muscle suit worn by Andy Lau became iconic, representing both physical and spiritual strength in a way that subverted typical action hero tropes.

The film's exploration of karma and destiny connects to other Hong Kong films of the era grappling with fate and identity, like **Final Destination** (2000) and **Turn Left, Turn Right** (2003). However, **Running on Karma** stands apart through its unique blend of metaphysical themes with crime genre elements, creating a template that influenced later works like **Re-cycle** (2006) and **The Detective** (2007). sections.content: The supernatural aspects of **Running on Karma** opened new possibilities for Hong Kong crime cinema. While films like **The Eye** (2002) and **A Chinese Ghost Story** (1987) had established supernatural elements in Hong Kong film, combining them with police procedural elements was revolutionary. This approach influenced later works like Mad Detective (2007) and **Detective Dee and the Mystery of the Phantom Flame** (2010).
